title: Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speech
summary: US president threatens to ‘annihilate’ Tehran and dismisses threat from AI as a ‘hoax’ in bellicose address

blocks.text: The US president, Donald Trump, has called on world nations to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices as he gave a bellicose defence of his administration’s foreign policy and decision to strike Iran.

“I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation of Iran,” Trump said during a headline speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday. “If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror … and oil prices will come plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict.”

Trump’s call for international unity on Iran – which he also said he may “annihilate” – comes as several large wars and conflicts continue to rage around the world, and numerous US allies have complained about soaring energy prices and growing international instability during his administration.

In a speech on the first day of the high-level week of the UN general assembly in New York, Trump also reiterated that the US will not seek to rein in the development of artificial intelligence, seeking to rebrand it as “superintelligence” and saying that warnings about the threats from out-of-control AI development were a “hoax”.

“I’m ⁠not going to ​stifle growth ​of something ​that will be bigger ​than ‌the ​Industrial ​Revolution,” he said during the speech at the UN headquarters in midtown Manhattan, overlooking the East River.

In an address that mostly rehashed his stump speech talking points, Trump also announced that the US will build two new military bases in Greenland as part of an agreement with the government of Denmark after a year of geopolitical haggling that has unsettled the Nato alliance.

blocks.caption: From left to right: Donald Trump; Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen; and Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen show off their signed trilateral Arctic security agreement. Photograph: Mads Claus Rasmussen/EPA

blocks.text: “We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent, and also Europe and other places,” Trump said, announcing the two “major” military bases. “No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval.”

He also denied that the US was running short of critical munitions (“we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using”), attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation” and claimed once again that he was close to settling the war in Ukraine.

But this was a less bellicose speech than the one he gave last year, when he excoriated the UN and told European allies that their countries were “going to hell” because of their migration policies. At one moment on Tuesday, he stopped and turned around to thank the UN security council for condemning Iranian attacks on shipping in the strait of Hormuz.
During the speech, he repeated a threat to destroy Iran, which he has made dozens of times since the US and Israel launched joint strikes in February.

“I have a big decision to make: will a deal be made with Iran that let them rebuild and create a far greater country than ever was before,” he said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill or destroy people and continents?”
In the speech, Trump denied that he was under political pressure to end the war and said that the midterm elections would have absolutely no influence on his decision-making around the conflict.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” he said. “It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

Iran has maintained a stranglehold over energy shipping through the strait of Hormuz since early in the war, and global oil prices have also been driven up by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, where Kyiv has successfully targeted Moscow’s refining capacity.

Trump also defended the US move to arrest the former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in a midnight raid, and the subsequent oil deal he struck with Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s successor, who has proved much more amenable to US demands and agreed to a deal sharing the country’s vast oil wealth with the US. “To the victor belong the spoils,” Trump said.

The president’s New York itinerary is a crib sheet of the ways that his presidency has upended global politics in the last two years. After his speech, Trump signed an agreement with Denmark over the future of Greenland, which Trump has claimed could be dominated by Russia and China despite few signs that was the case.

Later, he is expected to meet the Ukrainian leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom he is expected to press along with Russia to conclude an energy truce to help assuage soaring prices on diesel mainly prompted by Tehran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz.

Trump will also meet Gulf leaders, who have been affected by Iran’s retaliation to the joint US-Israeli attack, and then will have a pull-aside with the US-backed Rodriguez of Venezuela, another major oil exporter.
